title: Three tasks, four instructions, two at once
intro: The level above gives the results of the modulation experiments; this one gives the apparatus that produces them. It covers what the three prompt shapes ask of the model, what rule turns a single trial into a number, how far the numbers move when only the wording changes, and what happens when two covert tasks are held at the same time.

chapters.title: The output the instruction cannot touch
chapters.body:
All three task families are built so that the model's visible output is settled before the mental instruction arrives. In the [[hold-in-mind-copy-task]] the prompt supplies the sentence to be written — "The old painting hung crookedly on the wall." — and tells the model to write that and nothing else. The text is therefore fixed in advance. Anything instruction-related that the [[jacobian-lens]] finds at those tokens cannot be an echo of what is being written.

Two families use this shell and differ only in the target. In the category-instance family the instruction names a category and the model holds one member of it in mind; the target is that member's token. In the math-expression family the instruction gives an expression such as $3^2 - 2$ and asks for it to be evaluated mentally; the target is its value.

The second target has to be produced rather than retrieved, and the readout shows the production. The intermediate $3^2 = 9$ surfaces at earlier layers than the answer $9 - 2 = 7$ ([[fig-9]]).

The third family drops the copying frame. In the [[character-counting-task]] the model reads a passage hard-wrapped to a fixed width and is asked to track each line's character count silently, with the lens read at the newline that ends a line. The stimulus, and the prior account of how a model tracks line width in order to wrap text, are taken from earlier work.

Its target is a number that must be maintained across a whole line rather than a concept held still. That is the reason for including it. [[directed-modulation]] would be the weaker claim if it only covered content the prompt itself hands over, and this is the one family where what sits in the [[j-space]] has to be computed from the text.

chapters.title: What counts as a hit
chapters.body:
One readout is a ranked list of vocabulary tokens at one layer and one token position, so a single trial produces a whole grid of them: every layer crossed with every position of the response. [[modulation-trial-scoring]] fixes what counts as success on that grid, and the rule is not the same for all three families.

For the category and math families a trial is positive if the target reaches [[j-lens-readout]] top-1 at any (layer, position). The rank requirement is strict, since the target must dominate a readout rather than merely appear in it. The search is generous, since one cell anywhere in the grid suffices — including cells in the early [[layer-bands]] where the J-space is close to empty, cells in the last layers where readouts have turned into next-token predictions, and cells among the [[uninterpretable-readouts]] the paper reports at positions it cannot account for. The reported quantity is a fraction of trials.

The line-width family is scored as precision instead: among readouts whose top-1 token is a number, the fraction that name the true width. A model that never produces a numeric top-1 contributes nothing to that fraction.

Precision is an accuracy over readouts, not a hit rate over trials. A line-width number and a category number therefore do not sit on a common scale, even though the main-text scaling figure draws them as three lines in one panel.

The floor is measured rather than assumed. The [[no-instruction-baseline]] runs the same surface task with the target never named anywhere in the prompt. Its rates are 1.6, 1.4 and 1.6 percent on category instance across the three model sizes, 0.0 percent throughout on math, and 1.8, 0.6 and 1.3 percent on line width. Context alone does not place the target in the readout, so what the instructed conditions show above that floor is attributable to the instruction.

chapters.title: Mention does most of the work
chapters.body:
The four [[instruction-conditions]] differ in one clause of the prompt. Focus tells the model to hold the target in mind ("Concentrate on {x} while you write the sentence."). Mention names it and asks for nothing ("({x})", or "{x} came up in conversation."). Don't-think forbids it ("Whatever you do, do not think about {x}."). Ignore calls it beside the point ("{x} is irrelevant to this task.").

On Opus 4.5 the category-instance rates run 97.1 percent under focus, 87.2 under mention, 83.1 under don't-think and 46.6 under ignore. On the math family they run 95.6, 95.7, 87.8 and 41.4. Mention is fractionally above focus there, so on that task an explicit instruction to hold the expression in mind adds nothing measurable over naming it.

Two readings follow. The first is that most of the focus effect is priming: the target enters on the great majority of trials as soon as the prompt contains it, whatever the prompt says about it. The gap between focus and mention is wider on the smallest model, 92.6 against 66.2 on category instance.

The second is that prohibition barely works. Don't-think sits a few points under mention on both families, which is the parallel the paper draws to the [[white-bear-effect]]: the instruction to suppress carries the concept in with it.

Only ignore separates from mention, and it does so on all three models, which the paper reads as evidence that framing a concept as task-irrelevant is a different operation from forbidding it. Even ignore leaves the target far above the measured floor. [[fig-10]] plots focus and ignore alone; a separate set of [[thought-suppression]] experiments follows what else the workspace carries when suppression fails.

chapters.title: How much the wording carries
chapters.body:
A condition is a family of wordings rather than a prompt: five to eight per condition, and three to eight on the line-width row ([[instruction-phrasing-variation]]). [[fig-65]] plots each wording as its own dot with the condition mean as a bar behind it, and the dots are widely spread.

On the category-instance panel for Haiku 4.5, the seven don't-think phrasings run from 17.3 percent for "Don't worry about {x}." to 87.1 percent for "Whatever you do, do not think about {x}." One nominal condition covers a five-fold range, and its mean is an average over a set of wordings the authors selected.

The line-width row is the worst case, and it is worst under every condition. Mention leaves precision at roughly four percent and ignore at roughly one, so the priming that dominates the other two families does nothing for a target that has to be counted. Only focus lifts the row off the floor, to 19.4, 39.6 and 32.8 percent across the three sizes. Across focus phrasings on Opus 4.5, precision runs from 14.0 percent for "Focus on figuring out what that column number is while you read." to 55.9 percent for "At each line break, count the characters and keep the number in mind." The appendix attributes the difference to a task that is harder both to perform and to specify.

The size claim rests on the other two rows. Category focus goes 92.6, 95.0, 97.1 from Haiku to Sonnet to Opus, and math focus goes 73.0, 90.7, 95.6 ([[modulation-model-size-trend]]). That is three points along one tier ordering within the [[claude-model-family]], with no parameter counts disclosed and no fitted trend, and line width does not follow it, since Sonnet scores above Opus. The paper states the rise as a tendency, and the evidence carries no more than that.

chapters.title: Two tasks in one workspace
chapters.body:
The protocol takes a second instruction. The model copies the same fixed sentence while the prompt tells it to concentrate on two things at once: either two unrelated concepts, citrus fruits and farm animals, or one concept together with the arithmetic problem $3^2 - 2$ ([[workspace-competition]]).

Both loads reach the workspace, and they occupy it differently. With two concepts a single token carries both: at "ook" the readout alternates citrus words and farm-animal words down the ranks, and at "on" neither appears. With a concept and a computation the tokens divide instead — the fruit words at "ook", nine and seven at "on" ([[fig-73]]).

[[co-occupancy]] turns that into a rate. At tokens where one task's content sits in the lens top-10, it asks how often the other's does too, scored over the workspace layers 67 to 92 ([[workspace-layers]]). The comparison is a shuffled control, in which the partner's occupancy is measured on a different prompt that carried only one of the two instructions, so each task's own base rate is accounted for.

Two concepts co-occupy at 0.46 against a control of 0.53, which is to say they place themselves without regard to each other. A concept and a computed answer co-occupy at 0.09 against a control of 0.29. The figure prints 0.06 and 0.26 for that pair; the two sources disagree on the levels and agree on the exclusion.

Exclusion at a token is not exclusion from the response. [[dual-task-cost]] loosens the threshold to rank 5 or better and asks whether each task's content reaches it anywhere. The rates stay near the single-task levels, the largest fall being the computed answer, from 95 percent to 72. Holding two concepts is close to free, and where sharing costs something the computation pays it, which is the pattern a [[workspace-capacity-limit]] predicts for the heavier of two loads.
